essence: Twenty-nine salutations perform the all-self: every stuff of the world — fire, moon, gods, still, moving — named as His, every verse landing bowed (whole song).

Each bow names Him by paradox pairs — cool fire and devourer, Veda-foe and Veda-maker, round's cause and foe, ever-bound and ever-free, all rites and rite-free — the namaḥ holding both poles (vv1-22).
The litany turns to close: from Him to His dread power-ring (v23), from knowing to embracing (v24), from victory-cries to shelter-surrender (vv25-29).

sections.SUMMARY: It performs contemplation of the all-self as twenty-nine salutations. Each verse names Śiva by a paradoxical pair — cool fire and devourer, Veda-breaker and Veda-maker, saṃsāra's cause and foe, ever-bound and ever-free, all rites and no rite — and the *namaḥ* addressed to both poles at once is itself the recognition that opposites coincide only in Him. The litany closes by turning from Him to His terrible powers (23), from knowing to embracing (24), and from victory-cries to refuge (29).

rasa.sthayibhava: śānta (tranquility) as contemplation of the all-self
rasa.justification: The sthāyibhāva is devotion (bhakti) in the mode of contemplation (paribhāvanā); the vyabhicāri is wonder (camatkāra) at opposites coinciding only in Him. The rasa is the tranquility of non-dual contemplation — twenty-nine salutations naming Śiva by paradoxical pairs, each namaḥ a recognition that opposites coincide only in Him. Abhinava's rasa theory frames this as śānta: the relish (camatkāra) of the Absolute as the all-self.
